evidence.title: Detecting Transthyretin Cardiac Amyloidosis With Artificial Intelligence: A Nonrandomized Clinical Trial
evidence.outcome: Model discrimination across racial/ethnic subgroups (Hispanic, non-Hispanic Black, non-Hispanic White)
evidence.effect: AUROC 0.85 internal and 0.82 (95% CI 0.81-0.83) external, with similar performance across Hispanic, non-Hispanic Black, and non-Hispanic White patients.
evidence.quote: It had good discrimination for ATTR-CM detection with an area under the receiver operator characteristic curve of 0.85 (5-fold cross-validation, 0.77-0.85) in the internal set and 0.82 (95% CI, .81-0.83) in the external test set with similar performance in Hispanic, non-Hispanic Black, and non-Hispanic White patients.
evidence.sample_unit: patients tested for amyloidosis after AI flag (of 256 eligible)

evidence.title: Evaluating equity in performance of an electronic health record-based 6-month mortality risk model to trigger palliative care consultation: a retrospective model validation analysis
evidence.outcome: Subgroup performance and fairness metrics on local retrospective data before deployment
evidence.effect: Subgroup analysis revealed higher FNR and lower FPR for black, Hispanic, younger, Medicaid/missing insurance, and low-SES patients, despite no consistent differences in c-statistic, ICI or Brier Score.
evidence.quote: An EHR-based mortality risk model was less likely to identify some marginalised patients as potentially benefiting from palliative care, with younger age pinpointed as a possible mechanism.

evidence.title: An artificial intelligence prediction model for optimizing patient selection for cardiac imaging for the investigation of suspected coronary artery disease
evidence.outcome: Model performance and impact across sex, age, ethnicity and marginalization subgroups
evidence.effect: Local model AUROC lowest for Black patients (0.612); after provincial updating ethnic differences narrowed (0.749-0.790). Benefit skewed to females (42/50 ICAs avoided vs 18/32 for males).
evidence.quote: The local model performed best for Asian patients (AUROC = 0.704 [95% CI: 0.702, 0.705]) and worst for Black patients (AUROC = 0.612 [95% CI: 0.609, 0.614]).
evidence.sample_unit: elective outpatients undergoing invasive coronary angiography

evidence.title: FairGlucose: A CGM Fairness Benchmark Reveals Subgroup Disparities Hidden in Population-Level Validation
evidence.outcome: Whether population-level validation reveals subgroup performance gaps versus subgroup-disaggregated analysis
evidence.effect: Population-level external validation concealed subgroup disparities (ratios 0.8 to 1.4; T1D vs T2D gap of 6 mg/dL, p<0.001) persisting across all 33 models.
evidence.quote: These findings establish that population-level validation alone is insufficient for equity assessment of digital health AI, motivating subgroup-disaggregated reporting as a default standard.

evidence.title: Hyperspectral imaging in the emergency department to characterize lower leg edema
evidence.outcome: Effect of skin pigmentation type on HSI classification accuracy
evidence.effect: No significant effect of skin type on classification accuracy across skin pigmentation types.
evidence.quote: Full-spectrum analysis substantially improved non-cellulitis edema versus healthy classification (patient-level AUC: 0.72 vs. 0.41; pixel-level AUC: 0.78 vs. 0.50), with no significant effect of skin type on accuracy.

evidence.title: AI-Human Hybrid Workflow Enhances Teleophthalmology for the Detection of Diabetic Retinopathy
evidence.outcome: AI discrepancy rates by age, sex, and race/ethnicity
evidence.effect: No significant association of discrepancies with age (P = 0.74), sex (P = 0.061), or White vs non-White race (P = 0.50); N = 1222.
evidence.quote: Artificial intelligence performance did not differ across age, sex, or self-reported race or ethnicity.

evidence.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of an Integrated AI Tool to Estimate Gestational Age From Blind Ultrasound Sweeps
evidence.outcome: Performance across prespecified patient subgroups, including high body mass index
evidence.effect: Performance was consistent in prespecified subgroups, including those with high BMI; the primary-window MAE was 3.2 (0.1) days vs 3.0 (0.1) days for the standard.
evidence.quote: Performance was consistent in prespecified subgroups, including the Zambia and North Carolina cohorts and those with high body mass index.

evidence.title: Evaluation of computer-aided detection for gastric cancer using white-light and linked-color imaging: a pilot study
evidence.outcome: False-positive detections by H pylori infection status
evidence.effect: WLI false positives: 5.1 (3.7), 10.6 (5.2), and 8.9 (4.6) for uninfected, current, and past infection; LCI: 1.9 (1.7), 5.6 (2.9), and 3.8 (2.3), respectively.
evidence.quote: In the state of H pylori infection, both LCI and WLI showed significantly higher false-positive rates for current and past infection cases than for uninfected cases.

evidence.title: Unverified Vendor Claims and Preventable Harms: A Mixed-Methods Longitudinal Independent Audit of Health AI System Performance in Nigeria
evidence.outcome: subgroup performance gaps in vulnerable groups
evidence.effect: Performance gaps were 28-38% larger among vulnerable groups, including a 38% higher Equity Harm Index for rural patients.
evidence.quote: Performance gaps were 28-38% larger among vulnerable groups (e.g., rural patients showed 38% higher EHI).

evidence.title: Current Use And Evaluation Of Artificial Intelligence And Predictive Models In US Hospitals
evidence.outcome: Share of hospitals using predictive models that locally evaluated them for bias
evidence.effect: Only 44 percent of hospitals using predictive models reported local evaluation for bias, compared with 61 percent for accuracy.
evidence.quote: Sixty-one percent of hospitals that used models evaluated them for accuracy using data from their health system (local evaluation), but only 44 percent reported local evaluation for bias.

evidence.title: Real-world performance evaluation of a commercial deep learning model for intracranial hemorrhage detection
evidence.outcome: AI performance across patient demographic subgroups
evidence.effect: Performance remained consistent across demographic subgroups.
evidence.quote: Performance was also reduced in the outpatient setting (72.2%), where subtle hemorrhages were more common, while remaining consistent across demographic subgroups.

evidence.title: Factors Impacting the Performance of Deep Learning Detection of Pulmonary Emboli
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR
evidence.outcome: Model performance differences across demographic subgroups (age, gender, race, BMI)
evidence.effect: Age, gender, race, and body mass index showed no significant associations with model performance.
evidence.quote: Demographic factors including age, gender, race, and body mass index showed no significant associations with model performance.

evidence.title: A Real-World Evaluation of LLM Medication Safety Reviews in NHS Primary Care
evidence.outcome: Persistence of failure patterns across patient demographic strata
evidence.effect: Failure patterns persisted across patient complexity and demographic strata, i.e., no subgroup was spared; not a subgroup-specific disparity.
evidence.quote: These patterns persisted across patient complexity and demographic strata, and across a range of state-of-the-art models and configurations.

evidence.title: Evaluating User Experiences with an AI Chatbot for Health-Related Social Needs: A Cross-Sectional Mixed Methods Study
evidence.outcome: Usability and trust differences across demographic subgroups
evidence.effect: Usability and trust were broadly consistent across most demographic groups, though participants with higher education and lower income showed modest decrements in usability.
evidence.quote: Regression analysis showed usability and trust were broadly consistent across most demographic groups, though participants with higher education and lower income showed modest decrements in usability.

evidence.title: AI Decision Support for Challenging Teledermatology Cases: MedGemma Performance in the Dermatology ECHO Program
evidence.outcome: Model accuracy variation across diagnostic categories
evidence.effect: Performance varied by category: 54.5% top-10 accuracy for Other diagnoses versus 0.0% for neoplastic conditions.
evidence.quote: Performance varied across diagnostic categories, with highest accuracy in Other categories (54.5%) and lowest in neoplastic conditions (0.0%).

evidence.title: Large language models outperform traditional natural language processing methods in extracting patient-reported outcomes in IBD
evidence.outcome: Model performance differences across demographic and diagnosis subgroups (fairness assessment)
evidence.effect: No biases were detected based on demographics or diagnosis.
evidence.quote: No biases were detected based on demographics or diagnosis.
evidence.sample_unit: clinic notes (50 UCSF test, 250 Stanford external validation)

evidence.title: Machine Learning and Real-World Data to Predict Lung Cancer Risk in Routine Care
evidence.venue: Cancer epidemiology, biomarkers & prevention : a publication of the American Association for Cancer Research, cosponsored by the American Society of Preventive Oncology
evidence.outcome: Model discrimination (xAUC) across racial and ethnic subgroups
evidence.effect: Model performed well temporally and externally, while performance was reduced for Asians and Hispanics.
evidence.quote: Model performed well temporally and externally, while performance was reduced for Asians and Hispanics.
evidence.sample_unit: individuals aged 45-65 in EHR development cohort

evidence.title: Fairness in the prediction of acute postoperative pain using machine learning models
evidence.outcome: Model performance and fairness across patient subgroups on local data
evidence.effect: Model biased for age, race (FPR 1.36-1.39 times higher for non-White), ADI (three of five metrics) and insurance type (three of five metrics).
evidence.quote: The model was biased against the patients with other (non-White) races in terms of FPR.

evidence.title: SCORE2 cardiovascular risk prediction models in an ethnic and socioeconomic diverse population in the Netherlands: an external validation study
evidence.outcome: Subgroup calibration and discrimination of SCORE2 by SES and ethnicity
evidence.effect: Underprediction was larger in low SES (OE 1.5 men, 1.6 women) and Surinamese subgroups (OE up to 2.5); discrimination moderate, C-statistics 0.63 to 0.76 across subgroups.
evidence.quote: Underprediction was larger in low socioeconomic subgroups of the overall study population (OE-ratio 1.5 and 1.6 in men and women, respectively), and comparable in Dutch and the combined "other ethnicities" low socioeconomic subgroups.

evidence.title: Adjusting FRAX Estimates of Fracture Probability Based on a Positive Vertebral Fracture Assessment
evidence.outcome: FRAX calibration in patient subgroups defined by VFA result and prior fracture
evidence.effect: FRAX underestimated risk in positive-VFA subgroups: with prior fracture MOF underestimated by 53% (multiplier 1.53) and hip by 76% (1.76); well calibrated in negative-VFA subgroups.
evidence.quote: In these individuals, FRAX underestimated MOF risk by 53% (recalibration multiplier: 1.53) and hip fracture risk by 76% (recalibration multiplier: 1.76).

evidence.title: The Subgroup Imperative: Chest Radiograph Classifier Generalization Gaps in Patient, Setting, and Pathology Subgroups
evidence.outcome: Performance differences across patient, setting, and pathology subgroups
evidence.effect: Decreased sensitivity for solitary findings (43%-65%), patients younger than 40 years (27%-39%), and emergency department patients (38%-60%); decreased specificity on normal radiographs with support devices (59%-85%).
evidence.quote: Algorithms showed decreased sensitivity for solitary findings (43%-65%), patients younger than 40 years (27%-39%), and patients in the emergency department (38%-60%) and decreased specificity on normal chest radiographs with support devices (59%-85%).

evidence.title: Impact of Residential Social Deprivation on Prediction of Heart Failure in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes: External Validation and Recalibration of the WATCH-DM Score Using Real World Data
evidence.outcome: WATCH-DM calibration (expected/observed ratio) across social deprivation index subgroups
evidence.effect: Overestimated risk in SDI groups 1-2 (E/O 1.38, 1.36); underestimated in groups 4-5 (0.95, 0.80). C statistic 0.62.
evidence.quote: The score C statistic was 0.62; WATCH-DM systematically overestimated heart failure risk in SDI groups 1 to 2 (expected/observed ratios, 1.38 and 1.36, respectively) and underestimated the heart failure risk in groups 4 to 5 (expected/observed ratios, 0.95 and 0.80, respectively).

evidence.title: Diagnosis and prognosis of abnormal cardiac scintigraphy uptake suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis using artificial intelligence: a retrospective, international, multicentre, cross-tracer development and validation study
evidence.outcome: Robustness of AI performance across demographic factors, tracers, scanners, and centres in an algorithmic audit
evidence.effect: Audit demonstrated robustness across demographic factors, tracers, scanners, and centres; no details of subgroup numbers in the abstract.
evidence.quote: The medical algorithmic audit demonstrated the system's robustness across demographic factors, tracers, scanners, and centres.

evidence.title: Doctor's Orders-Why Radiologists Should Consider Adjusting Commercial Machine Learning Applications in Chest Radiography to Fit Their Specific Needs
evidence.outcome: Influence of sex, age, multimorbidity on DL-radiologist agreement
evidence.effect: In gold-standard negatives, multimorbidity (β=0.151), age (β=0.089) and sex (β=-0.038) significantly influenced DL results; in positives, female sex (β=0.153, p=0.026) linked to lower DL results.
evidence.quote: Significant effects were found for the parameters of multimorbidity ( β = 0.151, p < 0.001), age ( β = 0.089, p < 0.001), and sex ( β = −0.038, p = 0.031; sex was dummy coded using “0” for male and “1” for female).

evidence.title: Evaluating the Performance and Bias of Natural Language Processing Tools in Labeling Chest Radiograph Reports
evidence.outcome: Performance differences across patient demographic subgroups
evidence.effect: Aggregate accuracy was high (88.7%-94.3% on MIMIC/IU for most tools), but subgroup analyses showed significant bias with poorer performance in older patients.
evidence.quote: Although commonly used NLP tools for chest radiograph report annotation are accurate when evaluating reports in aggregate, demographic subanalyses showed significant bias, with poorer performance in older patients.

evidence.title: Cross-institutional validation of a polar map-free 3D deep learning model for obstructive coronary artery disease prediction using myocardial perfusion imaging: insights into generalizability and bias
evidence.venue: European journal of nuclear medicine and molecular imaging
evidence.outcome: AI performance differences across patient subgroups (stress type, age)
evidence.effect: Performance lower in treadmill stress MPI patients in the internal cohort and in patients over 70 years old in the external cohort.
evidence.quote: The performance was lower in patients who underwent treadmill stress MPI in the internal cohort and in patients over 70 years old in the external cohort.

evidence.title: Dual site external validation of artificial intelligence-enabled treatment monitoring for neovascular age-related macular degeneration in England
evidence.outcome: subgroup error distribution
evidence.effect: No significant error differences; accuracy: age 78.6–84.6%, sex 79.9–81.7%, ethnicity 79.5–87.1%, diabetes 74.6% vs 81.8%.
evidence.quote: The distribution of errors from R9 did not appear to differ significantly between subgroups defined by age, sex, ethnicity or diabetic status (Table 2 ).

evidence.title: Evaluating the impact of data biases on algorithmic fairness and clinical utility of machine learning models for prolonged opioid use prediction
evidence.outcome: Subgroup performance disparities in external validation and after retraining
evidence.effect: Stage 2 disparities: opioid-naive 0.68 vs opioid-exposed 0.63, Hispanic 0.68 vs non-Hispanic 0.70; disparities persisted for opioid-exposed after retraining.
evidence.quote: Predictive performance in Stage 1 was equal across groups, but Stage 2 showed disparities: Hispanic 0.68 vs non-Hispanic 0.70 ( P < .001), opioid-naive 0.68 vs opioid-exposed 0.63 ( P < .001), depression 0.68 vs non-depression 0.69 ( P < .001), and mild comorbidity 0.71 vs severe comorbidity 0.69 ( P < .001).

evidence.title: AI-Powered Chest X-Ray for Diagnosing Pulmonary Tuberculosis in County and Township Health Care Facilities in Yichang: Retrospective, Real-World Study
evidence.outcome: CAD performance across subgroups (age, sex, region, patient category)
evidence.effect: CAD outperformed radiologists in all subgroups; age ≥80 less likely to have high PPV (OR 0.21, 95% CI 0.10-0.44); no sex or inpatient/outpatient differences.
evidence.quote: Multivariate logistic regression also demonstrated that advanced age (≥80 y) groups were less likely to achieve high PPV (OR 0.21, 95% CI 0.10‐0.44; P <.001).

evidence.title: Large Language Models for Psychiatric Diagnosis Based on Multicenter Real-World Clinical Records: Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: LLM diagnostic accuracy across age subgroups
evidence.effect: Accuracy varied by age group: highest in older adults (up to 79.5%), lower in adolescents.
evidence.quote: Diagnostic performance varied across age groups, with the highest accuracy observed in older adult patients (up to 79.5%) and lower accuracy in adolescents.

evidence.title: External validation of the PREVENT risk score: performance and clinical utility in an Iranian population
evidence.outcome: Sex-specific discrimination and calibration performance
evidence.effect: AUC 0.84 (0.82-0.86) in women vs 0.76 (0.74-0.78) in men; risk underestimated in men but not women.
evidence.quote: Using the published 10-year logistic PREVENT equations, discrimination was higher in women (AUC 0.84 [0.82–0.86]) than in men (AUC 0.76 [0.74–0.78]) (Fig. 1 ).
evidence.sample_unit: adults in a community-based cohort (Tehran Lipid and Glucose Study)

evidence.title: Multicenter validation and updating of the ELDER-ICU model for severity assessment in elderly critical illness
evidence.outcome: AUROC across sex, age, ethnicity, ICU type, and CCI subgroups
evidence.effect: Sex differences were negligible in US and Austria but pronounced in Asian sites. Estimates for Black, Asian, and Hispanic subgroups were unstable because of small samples. Surgical ICUs had higher AUROC than MICU.
evidence.quote: Sex-based differences were negligible in the US and Austrian cohorts but pronounced in the Asian sites, where AUROCs were consistently higher among females than males.
evidence.sample_unit: ICU patients aged 65+ across eight representative validation cohorts (Table 1)
evidence.country: United States, Austria, South Korea, China

evidence.title: Performance of PREVENT Cardiovascular Risk in Electronic Health Record-Based Clinical Practice
evidence.outcome: Subgroup discrimination and calibration by race, ADI, and insurance
evidence.effect: C-index lowest in Black individuals, highest ADI quartile, and Medicare patients; calibration worse for disadvantaged subgroups.
evidence.quote: Asian males showed the highest C-index, and Black individuals showed the lowest.

evidence.title: Comparative performance of risk prediction models for kidney disease: an external validation using 0.5 million UK Biobank participants
evidence.outcome: Model discrimination across subgroups (age, sex, ethnicity, diabetes, hypertension)
evidence.effect: Discriminative performance was poorer for people with diabetes or hypertension.
evidence.quote: Discriminative performance was poorer for people with diabetes or hypertension.

evidence.title: Investigation of Concordance between Artificial Intelligence and Manual Measurements of the Cardiac Parameters in Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging
evidence.venue: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
evidence.outcome: Sex-stratified agreement between AI and manual cardiac MRI measurements
evidence.effect: AI-manual agreement was good to excellent in males and the whole cohort (ICCs 0.551-0.922), but females showed greater variability; segmental wall thickness was weaker in females.
evidence.quote: Female subjects showed greater variability.

evidence.title: External Evaluation Reveals Reduced Performance of the PathFX Survival Model in 1018 Patients With Extremity Metastases
evidence.outcome: PathFX performance differences across sex, race and treatment-period subgroups
evidence.effect: Better discrimination in females and poorer performance with flatter calibration slopes in patients who were not White; no clear differences by treatment period.
evidence.quote: The subgroup analyses suggested heterogeneity; that is, the model exhibited a better discrimination in females and poorer performance in patients who were not White with flatter calibration slopes.

evidence.title: Leveraging ECG foundation models in critical care for sinus rhythm and atrial fibrillation classification
evidence.outcome: Model performance stratified by sex and age subgroups
evidence.effect: Minimal differences between sexes and greater variability across age groups for AF than SR, attributed to small uneven subgroup sizes rather than genuine bias.
evidence.quote: Demographic analyses showed minimal differences between sexes and greater variability across age groups for AF than for SR, again likely reflecting uneven and small subgroup sizes rather than genuine model bias (Figure 5 ) [ 35 ].

evidence.title: Mobile-accessible deep learning-based self-assessment tool for measles screening in low-resource settings
evidence.outcome: Model performance across annotated subgroups (skin tone, age, body region) in internal and external validation
evidence.effect: TNRs ranged 79.0% to 92.9% in external datasets; lower TPR for Fitzpatrick type IV (77.8%) and upper extremities (80.0%); lower TNR in children under 5 (67.2%), torso (68.0%), neck (71.7%).
evidence.quote: Lower true positive rates were observed for images with Fitzpatrick type IV skin tones (77.8%) and lesions on the upper extremities (80.0%).
evidence.country: Multiple/international (image datasets from public sources; not country-specific)

evidence.title: Predictive Performance Precision Analysis in Medicine: Identification of low-confidence predictions at patient and profile levels (MED3pa I)
evidence.outcome: High-misclassification patient profile
evidence.effect: MED3pa identified a patient profile with high misclassification risk.
evidence.quote: In the clinical example, MED3pa identified a patient profile with high misclassification risk, demonstrating its potential for safer deployment.

evidence.title: A Mobile AI-enhanced Platform for Standardized Wound Assessment and Clinical Decision Support
evidence.outcome: AI performance stability across skin tone categories and imaging conditions
evidence.effect: Performance remained stable across skin tone categories and imaging conditions; dataset included 32% Monk Skin Tone 7-10.
evidence.quote: Performance remained stable across skin tone categories and imaging conditions.

evidence.title: Data leakage inflates reported accuracy of deep learning for kidney stone detection on CT: a leakage-free, calibrated and uncertainty-aware reassessment across three centers
evidence.outcome: Sex disparity in sensitivity after pooling across patients
evidence.effect: No sex disparity in sensitivity found once pooled across patients, though one appeared spuriously at the image level.
evidence.quote: no sex disparity in sensitivity was found once results were pooled across patients, though one appeared spuriously at the image level.

evidence.title: A framework for evaluating clinical artificial intelligence systems without ground-truth annotations
evidence.outcome: Model performance differences by skin tone (Fitzpatrick I-II vs V-VI) on dermatology images
evidence.effect: Ground-truth NPV was 0.83 vs 0.78 for skin tones I-II vs V-VI; SUDO AUC 0.60 vs 0.58, both indicating bias favouring I-II.
evidence.quote: Our findings demonstrate that both SUDO and the traditional approach (with ground-truth labels) identified a bias in favour of patients with a Fitzpatrick scale of I-II, which is consistent with previously-reported bias findings 14 .
evidence.sample_unit: data points (images, patches, reviews, clinical note samples)

evidence.title: Distribution shift detection for the postmarket surveillance of medical AI algorithms: a retrospective simulation study

evidence.quote: For example, the referable DR detection performance for different ethnicities ranged between 0.50 and 0.79 sensitivity, and classification performance in all metrics was reduced for images with lower quality.

evidence.title: Machine learning for personalized antimicrobial susceptibility breakpoints
evidence.outcome: AUROC of UTI prediction models across race, sex, and age subgroups
evidence.effect: Overall performance similar across groups, but smaller groups showed larger differences; urine model AUROC 0.56-0.73 by race, 0.40 for ages 10-19, 0.52 for 90-99.
evidence.quote: The fairness analysis revealed that while overall model performances were similar across demographic groups, some smaller groups had larger performance difference compared with the average value—this may be due to an insufficient sample size for robust model training.
evidence.sample_unit: patients (urine culture dataset; 1947 in blood culture dataset)

evidence.title: Development and multicentre validation of an artificial intelligence electrocardiogram model for ventricular remodeling in repaired tetralogy of Fallot
evidence.outcome: AUROC across subgroups by sex, race/ethnicity, and age
evidence.effect: No difference by sex (P=0.18) or race/ethnicity (P=1.0); lower AUROC in <22 years vs older (0.73 vs 0.85; P=0.005).
evidence.quote: There was lower performance in children and young adults <22 years old vs. older adults (AUROC 0.73 vs. 0.85; P = 0.005).

evidence.outcome: Performance on minority diabetes subtype classes
evidence.effect: Top model misclassified 61% of GDM and 42% of SD cases as T2DM; balanced-subset F1 peaked at 77.39% vs 0.951 on imbalanced data.
evidence.quote: A confusion matrix analysis revealed the top-performing model (DeepSeek-V3, Chinese Prompt 1) suffered from significant class imbalance, misclassifying high proportions of minority classes like GDM (61%) and SD (42%) as T2DM.

evidence.outcome: Subgroup AUROC and specificity across comorbidities
evidence.effect: AFIB/flutter AUROC 0.875, specificity 0.578; LBBB AUROC 0.859, specificity 0.219; IHD specificity 0.596.
evidence.quote: In patients with AFIB or flutter, the AUROC decreased to 0.875 (95% CI 0.858‐0.890), accompanied by a reduction in specificity to 0.578 (95% CI 0.564‐0.592) and PPV to 0.174 (95% CI 0.158‐0.190).

evidence.outcome: AUC across BI-RADS density subgroups on CBIS-DDSM
evidence.effect: ResNet-50 D1 0.912 to D4 0.842; Mammo-FM D4 0.870 vs ResNet-50 0.842 (n=140, CIs overlap); all models lose AUC as density increases.

evidence.title: Transferring healthcare risk prediction models between Medicaid populations: a transfer learning evaluation
evidence.outcome: Subgroup performance disparities of risk model in target population
evidence.effect: Native American subgroup (n=53) TPR 0.200 for meta-ensemble and target-only, missing most true cases; source-only TPR 0.867 with FPR 0.921.
evidence.quote: The Native American subgroup ( n = 53 in test set) showed highly variable performance across models: source-only achieved high TPR (0.867) but also very high FPR (0.921), indicating near-indiscriminate positive predictions for this group; meta-ensemble (TPR = 0.200) and target-only (TPR = 0.200) showed very low TPR, effectively missing most true cases.
evidence.sample_unit: Virginia Medicaid members in hold-out test set

commentary.bottom_line: Four studies, three of them offline, suggest that subgroup analysis on local data can reveal performance gaps that aggregate metrics and population-level validation miss. No study compared patient outcomes between deployments that did and did not include local subgroup validation.

perspectives.view: One prospective deployment tested 50 of 256 eligible patients after an AI flag, and three offline or benchmark studies applied subgroup analysis. All four support the practice, but they measure gap detection rather than patient outcomes. Hazard studies are split, and several found no subgroup differences. This suggests that gaps vary by tool and site, which argues for checking locally.

In one local analysis of 58,464 encounters, c-statistic, ICI, and Brier score showed no consistent differences, yet false negative rates were higher for Black, Hispanic, younger, Medicaid, and low-SES patients. A benchmark of 33 models found that population-level validation concealed subgroup disparities. A hazard study reported aggregate accuracy of 88.7% to 94.3% alongside poorer performance in older patients.

In a Canadian cohort of 319,012 patients, local model AUROC was lowest for Black patients (0.612). After provincial updating, the ethnic range narrowed to 0.749-0.790. This suggests that subgroup findings can inform model updating before use. None of the four studies reported the analyst time, data preparation burden, or sample sizes needed for stable subgroup estimates.

The one test that included Medicaid and low-income patients found higher false negative rates in those groups. A separate hazard study found false positive rates 1.36 to 1.39 times higher for non-White patients and bias by area deprivation and insurance type. That study included limited English proficiency and low health literacy patients, but it did not test the practice.

A survey of US hospitals found that 44 percent of those using predictive models evaluated them locally for bias, compared with 61 percent that evaluated accuracy. This suggests many systems would need new capacity to adopt the practice. No study reported the cost, staffing, or time required to run subgroup fairness analyses before deployment.

Subgroup analysis in the Canadian angiography study found that benefit skewed to females, with 42 of 50 procedures avoided compared with 18 of 32 for males. Findings like this may show patients and clinicians which groups a tool serves less well. None of the four tests of the practice measured patient trust or patients' access to a human reviewer.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared deployments with and without local subgroup validation on patient outcomes, missed diagnoses, or disparity trends after go-live. Studies are also needed on the minimum local sample sizes for reliable subgroup estimates, on the resources the analysis requires, and on how often vendor bias reports disagree with local results.
commentary.underserved_note: One offline test (pmid:37001995) included Medicaid, low-income, and racial and ethnic minority patients and found higher false negative rates in those groups, and the Canadian test analyzed marginalization subgroups. No test of the practice included limited English proficiency, low-literacy, or explicitly safety-net populations. Whether local subgroup validation detects gaps for these groups therefore rests on hazard studies rather than on tests of the practice.
